newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Turkmen leader upset by sour Russian Gazprom talks.
newsitem.headline: Turkmen leader upset by sour Russian Gazprom talks.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov said on Thursday his relations with the head of Russian gas monopoly Gazprom, on whose pipelines his Central Asian state heavily relies, took a turn for the worse this week.

Niyazov held talks with Gazprom chief executive Vyakhirev and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Wednesday to try to resolve a dispute which has forced the impoverished desert nation to sharply curtail its gas exports and output.

"Yesterday in talks with Viktor Stepanovich (Chernomyrdin) and with Rem Vyakhirev, I felt the smell of old Soviet ambitions, when they said, OK, we can do without your gas," Niyazov told a news briefing.
"I also said OK, we can also do without you. That's why I was a little upset yesterday."

Vyakhirev last week told Interfax news agency that Gazprom may break off ties with Turkmenistan altogether, adding that Gazprom itself may supply gas-guzzling Ukraine's needs in future rather than ship Turkmen gas there.
Turkmenistan itself decided to cut exports to Ukraine in March, when Ukraine failed to pay off gas debts in the range of $1 billion.
But Gazprom also curtailed Turkmen gas deliveries to other countries in the Commonwealth of Independent States and more importantly to hard-currency markets in Europe.
This was despite a deal signed by the two sides in late 1996 in which Turkmenistan was could export 20 billion cubic metres of gas to Europe annually and another 20 bcm to CIS countries.

Turkmenistan relies wholly on Gazprom to get its gas to Europe, and the breakdown in relations between the two sides has sent its gas output tumbling. It produced just 0.55 bcm in June compared with 2.69 bcm in March.

Niyazov's defiant stance on Gazprom may be partly explained by the fact that the former Soviet republic is opening a new export route south to Iran. He said he hoped deliveries would start in October.
Niyazov also said Turkmenistan, which has huge natural gas reserves estimated at 21 trillion cubic metres, would sell additional volumes to Kazakhstan.
But these exports will only go a small way to covering for the losses caused by the breakdown in relations between Turkmenistan and Ukraine and Gazprom.
Niyazov said he reached broad agreement with Russian President Boris Yeltsin on oil and gas questions when the two leaders met in the Kremlin on Thursday.
But in the short term at least, it is even more important for the cult leader to strike a deal with Vyakhirev.
